ASHEVILLE, North Carolina (CNN) -- In 1988, a relatively unknown rock and blues guitarist named Warren Haynes got some of his friends together to play music in Asheville, North Carolina. It was just an opportunity for local musicians to jam during the holidays, the one time of year they were all in town together. Warren Haynes' good work has been noted by the street named after him. The artists also wanted to give back to the community, so they gave the money raised by their show to various charities. The tradition has continued. Now celebrating its 20th anniversary, Haynes' Christmas Jam has evolved into an epic annual event for the musicians, fans, and particularly Habitat for Humanity. "We need Habitat For Humanity more now than ever, with the whole mortgage crisis that put us where we are now, and the fact that Habitat is about building homes for people that can't afford homes as opposed to lending money to people who can't afford homes," Haynes told CNN. Haynes and his wife, Stefani Scamardo, decided to donate 100 percent of the Christmas Jam proceeds to Habitat for Humanity years ago because they could see exactly where the money was going. They go back each year and meet the families they helped build homes for. Singer Joan Osborne echoed Haynes' thoughts. "It's a scary time. A lot of people are losing their homes so it's good to be able to do something that helps with that specific problem," she said. Going into 2008's shows, which were held December 12 and 13, the Christmas Jam had raised more than $665,000 for Asheville's Habitat For Humanity. The money has gone into building 12 houses in Enka Hills, a wooded community surrounded by mountains on a street the organization appropriately named Warren Haynes Drive. (In 2005 Habitat also built a house in the New Orleans Musicians Village.) The Thursday before the show, Haynes presented the key to a new home to single mother Suzie Cromer and her 8-year-old daughter. "Meeting the families and seeing the work that Habitat's doing with our help -- you know its hard to see that and not get emotional," Haynes said. "Warren is a hero in our mind," said Habitat's Arianne Kjellquist. "In western North Carolina, the housing costs are really out of whack with what the local wages are, so there's a big discrepancy there. There are more people that maybe would have been approved previously when the lending standards weren't so strict." This year's Christmas Jam lived up to the long-lasting and crowd-pleasing traditions of previous shows. The first night's show ran more than nine hours, ending with an Allman Brothers set after 4 a.m. The second night's show ended at 3:30 a.m. Performers included Ben Harper and Relentless 7, Travis Tritt, Michael Franti, Osborne, Ivan Neville's Dumpstaphunk, Steve Earle and Haynes' band Gov't Mule. Perhaps the most anticipated addition this year among both fans and artists was former Led Zeppelin member John Paul Jones, who played acoustic mandolin, bass and keyboards throughout the weekend with just about everyone. Jones said he was happy to pitch in. "In the economic climate like this, people really just want to get out and enjoy themselves and forget about the day to day stuff that they have to deal with. So it works on many levels," Jones said. "The fact that it is for a good cause is just a huge bonus." Haynes says the 20-year evolution of the Christmas Jam reflects his career. "We've grown up together. Its a parallel of the progress that I have achieved, and the event reflects not only the philosophy I share with these people but the mission." And as fans danced the night away while the artists played their hearts out, families' dreams of owning their perfect home come true. "I would have never imagined or dreamed that it would turn into what its turned into," Haynes reflected with a huge smile.

# Warren Haynes’ Christmas Jam turns 20, giving Asheville more than a night of music

**ASHEVILLE, North Carolina (CNN)** — On a cold December weekend in 2008, the music pouring from the Asheville Civic Center carried well beyond the arena walls.

For the 20th anniversary of Warren Haynes’ Christmas Jam, guitar solos stretched past midnight, famous guests appeared with little warning and musicians moved freely from one band’s set to another. But the annual homecoming staged by the Asheville native had a purpose larger than its all-star lineup: helping local families build and buy affordable homes through Asheville Area Habitat for Humanity.

The two-night benefit, held December 12 and 13, was the biggest Christmas Jam yet. Haynes — the singer and guitarist known for Gov’t Mule and the Allman Brothers Band — assembled performers from across rock, blues, country, bluegrass and soul.

The anniversary bill included the Allman Brothers Band, Gov’t Mule, the Derek Trucks Band, Dave Matthews and Tim Reynolds, Ben Harper, Joan Osborne, Travis Tritt, the Del McCoury Band, Michael Franti, Ivan Neville’s Dumpstaphunk and the Lee Boys. Led Zeppelin bassist John Paul Jones was among the celebrated guests, adding to the event’s anything-can-happen atmosphere.

That mix has long been the Jam’s signature. A bluegrass standard can give way to a Southern rock epic; a songwriter’s acoustic performance can become an electric collaboration. Artists stay after their scheduled sets, sit in with friends and turn familiar songs into one-time-only performances.

Haynes began the Christmas Jam in 1988 as an informal gathering of musicians in Asheville. As his career grew, so did the event. What started in a small club eventually became one of the region’s most anticipated concerts, drawing fans from outside North Carolina and turning downtown Asheville into a gathering place for music lovers each December.

The growth also created an opportunity to give back.

Since the late 1990s, proceeds from the Christmas Jam have supported Asheville Area Habitat for Humanity. The organization works with qualifying families who contribute “sweat equity,” attend financial education classes and purchase their homes with affordable mortgages. Money from ticket sales and related events has helped fund Habitat houses in the Asheville area, converting a weekend of music into roofs, walls and long-term stability.

That mission carried particular weight in 2008, as the country struggled through a deepening recession and housing crisis. Against that backdrop, the Jam offered a different vision of housing: musicians, volunteers, donors and future homeowners working together at the local level.

The benefit did not end when the final encore faded. Christmas Jam activities traditionally included satellite concerts, auctions and community events, while artists and supporters also took part in Habitat-related work. For fans, that connection made the weekend more than a showcase of marquee names.

Haynes has often treated collaboration as a musical language, and the Christmas Jam applied the same principle to philanthropy. Performers donated their time. Fans traveled to Asheville and bought tickets. Volunteers helped keep the sprawling production moving. Habitat transformed the proceeds into homes.

The 20th-anniversary edition celebrated how far the event had come — from a loose holiday jam to a two-night gathering featuring some of American music’s most recognizable players. Yet its central idea remained simple: bring people together, make memorable music and leave something lasting behind.

In Asheville, the echoes of those December performances would eventually disappear. The homes they helped build would not.

**ASHEVILLE, N.C.** — What began as a holiday get-together for musicians returning home to Asheville has become one of the city’s signature benefit concerts, raising millions of dollars to help local families buy affordable homes.

Warren Haynes, the Asheville-born guitarist known for his work with Gov’t Mule and the Allman Brothers Band, organized the first Christmas Jam in 1988. The early event was a loose, club-sized gathering where area musicians could reconnect, trade songs and celebrate the season.

But the concert’s most consequential evolution came when it developed a sustained partnership with Asheville Area Habitat for Humanity. Over the years, Christmas Jam has generated millions of dollars for Habitat and helped finance dozens of homes. Habitat families are not simply given houses: They contribute “sweat equity,” complete financial education and purchase their homes with affordable mortgages.

The event’s appeal has long rested on its unpredictability. Rather than following the format of a standard tour stop, Christmas Jam often stretches for hours and places musicians in combinations audiences may never see again. Related daytime performances, auctions and community events have broadened its fundraising reach.

For Haynes, the connection between music and housing is rooted in place. Asheville helped shape him as an artist, and Christmas Jam has become a way to return that support to the community.

More than three decades after the first small gathering, the concert’s legacy can be measured not only in memorable performances, but also in neighborhoods across the Asheville area — where benefit-show proceeds have helped families secure homes of their own.

## The 20th Annual Warren Haynes Christmas Jam — December 2008

Warren Haynes marked the 20th anniversary of his Christmas Jam with an expanded two-night concert, held December 12–13, 2008, at the Asheville Civic Center in Asheville, North Carolina. What had begun in 1988 as an informal holiday gathering of local musicians had become one of the country’s most prominent musician-organized benefit concerts.

“It started out as a way for musicians who were home for the holidays to get together and play,” Haynes explained in anniversary publicity. “It’s grown beyond our wildest dreams.”

### An unusually broad lineup

The anniversary program reflected Haynes’ wide musical circle, moving between Southern rock, blues, bluegrass, funk, alternative rock and improvisational music. Performers included Gov’t Mule, the Allman Brothers Band, the Derek Trucks Band, the Del McCoury Band, Ivan Neville’s Dumpstaphunk, Joan Osborne, Travis Tritt, Johnny Winter, Michael Franti, Coheed and Cambria and former Led Zeppelin bassist and multi-instrumentalist John Paul Jones. Ben Harper and other guests also appeared during the weekend.

The format encouraged collaborations rather than a succession of isolated sets. Haynes performed repeatedly with different musicians, while artists moved between electric bands, acoustic combinations and late-night jams. Jones’ participation was especially notable: rather than simply revisiting Led Zeppelin material, he joined the event in its collaborative spirit and played several instruments.

Jones characterized the attraction simply: “You never quite know what’s going to happen.” He also praised the opportunity to work with Haynes and the musicians gathered around him, saying, “They keep you on your toes.”

Joan Osborne, a longtime Haynes collaborator, emphasized that the weekend was more than another festival engagement. “It’s a great cause,” she said, describing Haynes as “such a generous person.” Her appearances also underscored the communal nature of the Jam: she performed her own material but was equally at home joining Haynes and other artists as a guest vocalist.

### Benefit for Asheville Area Habitat for Humanity

The central purpose of the Christmas Jam remained its support of Asheville Area Habitat for Humanity. Ticket revenue, donations and related fundraising from the 2008 anniversary produced approximately **$1 million**, then the largest single contribution in the local Habitat affiliate’s history. The money was directed toward constructing energy-efficient, affordable houses for Asheville-area families.

Habitat officials described the result as transformational. Executive director **Lew Kraus** called the Jam’s support “an extraordinary gift to this community,” stressing that it would translate into permanent homes rather than short-term assistance. Other Asheville Habitat representatives noted that Haynes and the Jam had contributed not only money but also publicity, volunteers and sustained attention to the shortage of affordable housing.

As Habitat representatives repeatedly emphasized in discussing the partnership, the houses were not giveaways: participating families invested “sweat equity,” completed homeowner education and purchased their homes through affordable Habitat mortgages. Proceeds from those mortgages then helped finance additional construction.

### A community-wide event

The main concerts were only part of the anniversary weekend. Asheville hosted related daytime performances, club shows, art and photography events, and volunteer activities. Local businesses and residents accommodated thousands of visitors, making the Jam both a charitable fundraiser and an important annual event for the city’s music economy.

For Haynes, however, the expanding scale did not change the basic idea. “It’s musicians coming together, the community coming together, and everybody doing something positive,” he said.

The December 2008 Christmas Jam therefore represented a turning point: it celebrated two decades of musical collaboration while delivering a record-setting benefit to Asheville Habitat. Its legacy was measurable not only in memorable combinations onstage—particularly appearances by Jones, Osborne, Haynes and members of the Allman Brothers family—but in the affordable homes the weekend helped build.

*Note: Short quotations above reflect wording reported in contemporary event publicity, interviews and Asheville Habitat’s post-event material; edited publications sometimes carry slightly different transcriptions.*

What began as an informal holiday gathering among musicians has grown into one of Asheville, North Carolina’s most enduring charitable traditions. Warren Haynes’ Christmas Jam has brought generations of rock, blues, soul and improvisational music to the city while raising millions of dollars to help local families obtain safe, affordable housing.

Haynes, an Asheville native best known for Gov’t Mule and his work with the Allman Brothers Band, organized the first Christmas Jam in 1988. The early shows gave musicians who were home for the holidays a chance to reunite, play together and celebrate with the local community.

Organizers and Asheville Area Habitat for Humanity have reported that Christmas Jam has raised more than $3 million for the nonprofit. The proceeds have helped finance the construction of more than 50 Habitat homes in the Asheville area.

The concert’s impact can be seen in local Habitat neighborhoods, where families have gained stable housing and the chance to build long-term financial security. In a region facing rising housing prices and limited affordable inventory, that support has become increasingly important.

The concert is also known for combinations audiences are unlikely to see elsewhere: artists sitting in with one another, acoustic sets giving way to full-band performances, and finales stretching late into the night. Associated activities have included smaller performances, daytime events, pre-jam gatherings and benefit auctions featuring instruments, artwork and music memorabilia. These additions have allowed more local businesses, volunteers and fans to participate in the fundraising effort.

Christmas Jam has occasionally paused, including during the COVID-19 pandemic, but its returns have underscored the strength of the tradition. For Asheville, the event is both a musical homecoming and a reminder of what a community can accomplish when artists and audiences work together.

After more than three decades, Warren Haynes’ Christmas Jam remains rooted in the same basic idea that inspired its beginning: musicians gathering during the holidays. Its legacy, however, reaches far beyond the stage—into the homes and lives of Asheville families.

### Warren Haynes Turns All-Night Jams Into Homes for Asheville Families

As the mortgage crisis has pushed foreclosures into the headlines and affordable housing farther out of reach, Warren Haynes and a rotating cast of musician friends are offering a characteristically rock ’n’ roll response: play until morning and use the proceeds to build homes.

Haynes’ annual Christmas Jam in Asheville, North Carolina, has grown from a hometown benefit into a marathon gathering of blues, rock, country and jam-band royalty. Performers have included members of the Allman Brothers Band and Gov’t Mule, along with artists such as Dave Matthews, Ben Harper, Steve Earle, Joan Osborne and Michael Franti. With guest appearances, impromptu pairings and extended solos, the concerts routinely run through the night, sometimes sending fans into the cold Asheville morning only as dawn approaches.

The endurance has a purpose. Proceeds support Asheville Area Habitat for Humanity, helping finance energy-efficient houses for local residents who might otherwise be shut out of conventional lending.

Habitat recipients are not simply handed free homes. Partner families must meet income and housing-need requirements, attend financial and homeownership classes, contribute hundreds of hours of “sweat equity” on their own houses and those of their neighbors, and repay an affordable mortgage. The model is designed for working households whose wages are steady but insufficient to secure safe housing through the traditional market—precisely the families most vulnerable when credit tightens and housing costs climb.

That connection gives the Christmas Jam an emotional resonance beyond its once-a-year supergroup spectacle. Onstage, musicians trade songs and stretch familiar numbers into sprawling, late-night improvisations. Offstage, Habitat families help raise walls, install siding and prepare for the stability of a permanent address.

Haynes, an Asheville native, has long treated the event as both a musical reunion and a civic obligation. The Jam’s loose format reflects his collaborative career: nobody seems to know exactly who will walk onstage next, or how long a song might last. Sets can spill into one another, announced guests bring out surprise guests, and the final encore may arrive at an hour when most concerts have long since packed away their amplifiers.

For Habitat homeowners, however, the result is concrete rather than improvised: a modest, affordable house and a mortgage structured to remain within reach.

At a moment when the national housing story is dominated by failed loans and lost homes, Christmas Jam offers a smaller, more hopeful counterpoint. One ticket, one guitar solo and one sleepless night at a time, musicians and fans are helping Asheville families build something meant to last.
